display_title: Official Review of Paper2591 by Reviewer JVhe

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors proposed a framework to make a fair and comprehensive comparison for discrete and continuous Dynamic Graph Neural networks (DGNN) on the dynamic link prediction task. Results are interesting as the heuristic methods can outperform more complicated and advanced DGNNs.
content.main_review:
Strength:
1. The paper is overall clearly written and easy to follow.
2. The paper provided some very interesting insights into dynamic link prediction and listed out some interesting future directions. 
Weakness/concerns:
1.	GNN is known to be capable of aggregating node features to inference. However, for all the datasets, node features are initialized randomly or by node degree. The conclusion is thus limited to graphs without rich node features.  
2.	Why do authors not use negative samples (with an equal number to the positive ones) when they are evaluating on valid and test sets? If negative samples are used for AUC, the problem occurred for false positive rate can be alleviated. Besides, it would be more intuitive to apply the hits@k metric if we wanted to know whether positive samples were ranked higher than negative samples.
3.	All the datasets used in this work are quite small, even the largest one only has 11k nodes.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of providing a fair and comprehensive comparison for the dynamic link prediction task in this work is interesting and meaningful but the experiments still deserve further completion to support the authors’ conclusion.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

replying_to: Replying to Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks on Dynamic Link Prediction
display_title: Official Review of Paper2591 by Reviewer q6Fs

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors aim to evaluate the performance of current graph neural networks (static, discrete dynamic, and continuous dynamic GNNs) and compared them to heuristic baselines. They did several experiments on 6 public datasets, and performed hyper parameters tuning on each of the model. The authors summarized their finding that simple link prediction heuristics often perform better than GNNs, and that hyper parameters including sliding window sizes greatly affect performance. They also concluded that dynamic GNNs consistently outperform static GNNs.
content.main_review:
The authors has raised an important question that we need a comprehensive assessment of the many different graph neural networks together with the heuristic baselines. It is not straight forward how to do this in a complete, fair and informative way. While the authors of this paper has made many efforts to shed lights upon this questions, I have a few questions here:

The writing of the current paper needs to be improved. For example, in section 2.1, the author tries to define temporal edges by the nodes they connect and the start and end time, etc. The definition here does not seem to be used later in the paper. In these cases, it is confusing what the authors want to convey through the definitions.
Also, after reading, I got the impression that the author discussed too much about the dataset imbalance and why PR-curve is a good metric with dataset imbalance, while this is a fairly well-known concept. The heavy discussion on dataset imbalance distracts the discussion on the purpose of the paper, which is their findings from the comparisons. 

Second, many published work has done extensive comparisons. One of the main contribution of this work is that they proposed a framework to compare discrete DGNNs to continuous DGNNs. Currently the description of how this is done is not clear and a bit confusing in the main text. I suggest moving some of the text of A.4.3 to make it more clear. Comparing continuous DGNNs to discrete DGNNs is not a problem with straight forward solution. It is also not clear to me the current proposal makes a fair comparison, as the continuous DGNNs generate node embeddings that perform well on continuous setting. They can be understandably not performing as well on predict discrete graph snapshots even thought the decoder is retrained on discrete graphs, unlike the discrete DGNN models which are trained to work on discrete graph settings. Therefore, it might not be surprising to see TGN and TGAT not performing well compared to other GNNs under this setting.

In addition, many kinds of discrete DGNNs have been developed by now. The authors have evaluated EGCN and GC-LSTM and made conclusions based on that. Given the variety of DGNNs been developed, it would be better to include more different types of DGNNs in the comparison to draw solid conclusions. 
The authors also mentioned that link prediction heuristics are better at ranking the links initially, and suggested incorporating heuristics into GNNs. It would be good to include some suggested designs/trials on this direction and see if the performance increases. One example given in the paper is the model by Sankar et al (2020). However, Sankar et al developed a discrete dynamic model with GAT+attention. I'm not sure which part contributes to "incorporating heuristics into GNNs"?

Minor typos:
Section 2.3, the first sentence, "...networks. Where there is.."
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors performed many comparisons across three different types of GNNs in addition to link prediction heuristics. While the comparisons generate some insights, the way comparisons have been done might need to be more thoughtful. It would also be good to include more representative models in the comparison to draw more solid conclusions.

replying_to: Replying to Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks on Dynamic Link Prediction
display_title: Official Review of Paper2591 by Reviewer e8bH

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper tried to conduct a comprehensive study between different methods of GNNs with a focus on Dynamic GNN (DGNN) on existing benchmark datasets. The authors observed that simple link prediction heuristics often perform better than GNNs and DGNNs,  different sliding window sizes greatly affect performance, DGNNs consistently outperform static GNNs
content.main_review:
I do not find any significant novel contribution in this work. I agree that doing a thorough comparison between models and developing understandings based on those experiments are super important in the field of science. However, I think dynamic GNNs are a specific narrow subdomain, thus the requirement of standardization and a framework for training could be a premature step.
Concerns:
1. The word benchmarking in the title gives an impression that authors are curating the datasets that are used for the model evaluation. However, those datasets were introduced in previous related papers. 
2. I am not totally convinced about the objective of creating a training framework. Are you going to publish a framework that will do a hyperparameter search for DGNN training and thus would be a standardized eval platform for future DGNN researchers? 
3.  Another interesting avenue could have been curating interesting and bigger size datasets for this task. (see https://ogb.stanford.edu/docs/home/ for reference).
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend rejecting this paper since the contributions are not significant enough to get published.

replying_to: Replying to Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks on Dynamic Link Prediction

content.title: Withdrawal and brief reply
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for taking the time to read and review our paper. While we are of the opinion that our work is valuable to the community, we recognize that the reviewers find the contributions to be not significant enough for ICLR. We have therefore decided to withdraw. We are delighted that some reviewers think our findings are interesting. We have read all the reviews carefully and will take on board this valuable feedback.

We'd like to briefly respond to some of the important points brought up in the reviews.
1. On the intention of this comparison. We will rename the paper to better reflect that our main aim is to perform a fair comparison of GNNs on dynamic link prediction, rather than a benchmark for future evaluation. In short, we aim to be more like Errica et al. [1], than Dwivedi et al. [2].
2. On the evaluation. We do not use negative sampling as evaluation metrics have a high variance when the negative set is undersampled. A 1 to 1 ratio is an extreme undersampling that makes the AUC very unstable, which in turn may lead to incorrect ordering of predictors. (see Figure 8 from Yang et al. [3]). This variance would affect hyperparameter optimization decisions; e.g. which epoch to select when applying early stopping, and which hyperparameter settings perform better. While this can be counteracted by running multiple runs, we opted to minimize variance where we could.
3. On what the challenge is. It was rightfully pointed out that implementing the models is not challenging. The challenge lies in performing a fair comparison. Enabling this comparison, and making the comparison comprehensive and fair is really the crux of this work. The comparison is challenging because, until now, the continuous DGNNs are trained and evaluated in ways that are only possible continuous graphs, and similarly discrete DGNNs for discrete graphs. Since we train continuous DGNNs on continuous graphs but evaluate on discrete graphs, a comparison is now possible. Reviewer q6Fs has made some excellent points, and has, among other things, pointed out that continuous DGNNs might be underperforming due to the way we move from the continuous to the discrete domain. This is true, and we acknowledge that alternative ways of comparing (e.g. training end-to-end) might be beneficial to the continuous DGNNs. We do however find it intensely interesting that the continuous DGNNs, despite these limitations outperform other GNNs in terms of AUC.
4. On large graphs. We agree that applying DGNNs on large graphs is important, but we consider it outside the scope of this work to scale up DGNNs. If only considering the number of nodes, the task appears to be deceptively small. The predictions are based on the number of links that can exist in the next snapshot. Any model must produce a score for every pair of nodes, for every snapshot. Thus the framework does not support much larger graphs than 11k nodes. Negative sampling would of course solve this issue but would come with the caveats explored by Yang et al. [3]. Without negative sampling, our framework in its current state is not able to support graphs much larger than 11k nodes.

[1] A fair comparison of graph neural networks for graph classification. 2020. https://openreview.net/forum?id=HygDF6NFPB
[2] Benchmarking graph neural networks. 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.00982
[3] Evaluating Link Prediction Methods. 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.04094
